opus.text:
Yeah, absolutely. Um, so thanks for having me, first of all. So, I guess the short version is that I kind of fell into this sideways. I didn't, you know, set out with a five-year plan or anything like that.

I grew up in a pretty small town, and, uh, nobody in my family did anything remotely close to what I do now. So when I went off to school, I actually started in a completely different direction — I was convinced I was going to go one way, and then about two years in I just... realized I was miserable. Which, in hindsight, was probably the most useful thing that could've happened.

So I switched, and that's really where things started clicking for me. After that I spent, gosh, the better part of a decade working on the practical side of it — a lot of hands-on stuff, a lot of learning by messing things up in public, honestly. And then a few years ago I started getting pulled more into the, um, the bigger-picture side. Strategy, teaching, talking to people who are where I was fifteen years ago.

And that's sort of what I do now. I still keep a foot in the day-to-day because I think you lose the thread if you don't. But yeah — that's me in a nutshell. Happy to go deeper on any part of that.

kimi.text: Sure, happy to. Well, first of all, thanks for having me on the show — I've been looking forward to this. So I guess the short version is that I grew up in a small town in the Midwest, and I was always one of those kids who was curious about everything, constantly taking things apart to see how they worked. I ended up going to school for journalism, and after college I spent a few years bouncing around at local newspapers before I found my way into documentary work, which is really where things clicked for me. Over the past fifteen years or so, I've been producing and directing stories that focus on ordinary people in extraordinary circumstances, and that's taken me all over the country and, honestly, all over the world. Along the way I've written a couple of books, done some teaching, and most recently I've been working on a project that looks at how small communities adapt when the main industry in town disappears. That's kind of the thread that runs through everything I do — I'm fascinated by how people reinvent themselves when the life they planned on doesn't quite work out.

fable.text:
Yeah, sure, and thanks for having me on. So the short version is I've spent most of my career somewhere in the space between engineering and product. I studied computer science in undergrad, and honestly I went in thinking I'd end up doing something pretty conventional, like backend infrastructure at a big company. And I actually did that for a few years. I was at a large tech company working on distributed systems, which was a great education, but it was pretty far removed from anything a real person would ever touch.

Then around, I want to say 2016 or 2017, I got really interested in speech and audio. It started as a side thing. I was messing around with early text-to-speech models on weekends, and at the time they were, frankly, not good. Very robotic, very flat. But you could see the trajectory, right? Every six months they got noticeably better, and I remember thinking, if this keeps going, the way we interact with computers is going to change a lot.

So I left the big company, joined a small startup doing voice work, wore about eight different hats there, and eventually ended up starting my own thing with a couple of former colleagues. Today I lead a team that's focused on, basically, how do you make a synthetic voice sound like an actual human, with the right emotion, the right pacing, the little imperfections that make it feel real. And then outside of work, I've got two kids, I play a very mediocre amount of guitar, and I have strong opinions about coffee. So that's me in a nutshell.
